query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of oxygen into a Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high‐entropy alloy (HEA) enhances its glass‐forming ability by promoting the formation of ordered oxygen complexes that hinder the nucleation of crystalline phases during rapid cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: A polycrystalline Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high‐entropy alloy prepared by arc melting and drop‐casting.
generation.intervention: Interstitial oxygen doping to form an oxygen-doped HEA variant (similar to the O-2 HEA) under otherwise identical casting conditions.
generation.conditions: Rapid solidification using water-cooled copper mould casting with similar heating and cooling rates as the original process (e.g., casting dimensions ~10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm), ensuring comparable thermal histories.
generation.structural_mediator: Ordered oxygen complexes formed within the HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: The formation of ordered oxygen complexes increases local lattice distortions and atomic packing frustration. This increased disorder is expected to inhibit crystalline nucleation during cooling (by raising the kinetic barrier to crystal formation), thereby enhancing the glass-forming ability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxygen-doped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA (O-2 HEA) will require a lower critical cooling rate to achieve an amorphous structure compared to the undoped HEA, exhibiting a larger fraction of the amorphous phase under the same processing conditions.
generation.baseline: The undoped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA exhibits conventional crystallization behavior when processed under the same rapid-cooling conditions.
generation.boundary: The enhancement is expected only within a limited range of oxygen contents; excessive oxygen may lead to oxide phase segregation and adverse effects. Moreover, the effect is specific to this HEA system where the atomic size disparities and mixing enthalpies favor formation of ordered interstitial complexes.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is plausible based on observed ordered oxygen complexes in similar HEAs, the extent to which glass-forming ability is enhanced (i.e., the reduction in the critical cooling rate and increase in amorphous fraction) remains uncertain and will require precise experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA samples with varying oxygen contents (including an undoped control) using arc-melting and rapid-cooling (drop casting into a water-cooled copper mold). Determine the critical cooling rate and the resulting phase constitution of each sample.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify amorphous vs crystalline phases
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to detect glass transition and crystallization events
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess microstructure
Measurement of the critical cooling rate required to suppress crystallization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped samples do not show a significantly lower critical cooling rate or higher amorphous phase fraction compared to the undoped HEA, or if they instead exhibit increased crystallinity or oxide segregation leading to degraded glass-forming behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
